short: The yearly return investors earn by buying the US government's 30-year bond today and holding it until it matures.
kid: Imagine lending your toy to a friend for a very, very long time. Because you must wait so long to get it back, you ask for a little treat every year while you wait.
detail: The 30-year Treasury yield is the yield to maturity on the US government's longest regularly issued bond, often called the long bond. Because investors lock up money for three decades, it reflects expected future short-term rates plus a term premium for inflation and fiscal uncertainty. It reacts less directly to Federal Reserve decisions than short-term yields and more to long-run inflation expectations, government borrowing needs and demand from pension funds and insurers. Its long duration makes the bond's price very sensitive: small yield moves cause large gains or losses. The US Treasury suspended new 30-year issuance from late 2001 until February 2006. A common confusion is to assume US mortgage rates track it; they follow the 10-year yield more closely, because most mortgages are repaid or refinanced well before 30 years.
example: Say the Treasury sells a 30-year bond with $1,000 face value and a 4.5% coupon. The holder receives $45 a year, paid as two $22.50 instalments, or $1,350 over 30 years, plus $1,000 at maturity. If market yields then rise by 0.5 percentage point and the bond's modified duration is 16, its price falls by roughly 16 × 0.5% = 8%.
formula: Approximate price change (%) = - Modified duration × Change in yield (percentage points)

short: The yearly return on the Indian government's most-traded 10-year bond; India's headline gauge of long-term borrowing costs.
kid: When the country needs to borrow, it promises to pay a little extra every year for ten years. The size of that little extra tells everyone how costly borrowing is right now.
detail: The 10-year G-sec yield is the yield to maturity on the benchmark 10-year Government of India security, usually the most liquid one, which is replaced by a newer issue from time to time. It is India's reference long-term rate: banks, companies, state governments and bond funds price borrowing and investments off it. The yield rises when bond prices fall and falls when they rise. It is driven by the RBI's policy rate and liquidity, inflation, the government's borrowing programme, crude oil prices, US yields and foreign investor flows, which grew after Indian bonds entered JP Morgan's emerging-market bond index in June 2024. A common confusion is to mix up yield and coupon: the coupon is fixed when the bond is issued, while the yield changes every day with the market price. For live levels, check the rates board.
example: Say a bond fund holds ₹100 crore of the benchmark 10-year G-sec, which has a modified duration of about 7. If the yield rises by 10 basis points (0.10 percentage point), the holding loses roughly 7 × 0.10% = 0.70% of its value, or about ₹70 lakh. A 10 basis point fall would add about the same amount.
formula: Price = Sum of (C / 2) / (1 + y / 2)^t for t = 1 to 20 + Face value / (1 + y / 2)^20, solved for the yield y (G-secs pay coupons every six months)

short: The inflation rate the bond market is quietly expecting, found by comparing an ordinary government bond's yield with an inflation-protected bond's yield.
kid: Imagine two piggy banks. One gets the same extra coin every year; the other gets extra coins only when sweets get pricier. The point where both feel equally good shows how much people think sweet prices will rise.
detail: The breakeven inflation rate is the difference between the yield on a conventional government bond and the real yield on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity, such as US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). If actual inflation over the bond's life equals the breakeven, both bonds deliver the same return; higher inflation favours the inflation-linked bond. Central banks and investors watch 5-year and 10-year breakevens, and the 5-year, 5-year forward rate, to judge whether inflation expectations stay anchored. A common confusion is to treat breakevens as a pure forecast: they also contain an inflation risk premium and a liquidity premium, because inflation-linked bonds trade less than ordinary ones, so breakevens can drop in a crisis even when inflation views have not changed. India has issued inflation-indexed bonds only occasionally and they trade thinly, so Indian breakevens are rarely quoted.
example: Say the 10-year US Treasury yields 4.3% and the 10-year TIPS has a real yield of 2.0%. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate is 4.3% - 2.0% = 2.3%. If inflation averages more than 2.3% a year over the decade, the TIPS holder comes out ahead; if it averages less, the ordinary Treasury does better.
formula: Breakeven inflation rate = Nominal government bond yield - Real yield on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity

short: The market where banks, companies and governments borrow and lend cash for short periods, from overnight up to one year.
kid: Sometimes a friend needs a few coins just until tomorrow, and another friend has spare coins today. They lend and pay back very quickly, with a tiny thank-you on top.
detail: The money market is the wholesale market for borrowing and lending funds for up to one year. Its main instruments include call money, repurchase agreements, tri-party repo (TREPS), treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. Banks use it to manage day-to-day liquidity, companies to fund working capital or park surplus cash, and governments to cover short gaps between spending and receipts. It is where a central bank's policy rate takes effect first: the RBI steers the weighted average call rate towards the repo rate through its liquidity operations, and other short-term rates follow. Money market instruments are generally low risk and easy to sell, but not risk-free, as the 2018 IL&FS defaults showed. Do not confuse it with the capital market, which deals in long-term funds such as shares and bonds, or with money market mutual funds, which invest in these instruments.
example: Say ABC Ltd has ₹50 crore of spare cash that it will need for salaries in three months. It parks the money in money market instruments earning 6% a year, which brings in about ₹50 crore × 6% × 3/12 = ₹75 lakh of interest before the cash is needed.

short: The interest rate at which Indian banks lend to each other overnight with no security pledged, in the call money market.
kid: At the end of the day, one shopkeeper has extra coins and another is a little short. The first lends coins until tomorrow morning and gets a tiny extra coin back for helping.
detail: In India, call money is unsecured lending between banks and primary dealers for one day; notice money runs from 2 to 14 days and term money from 15 days to one year. Deals are mostly struck on the NDS-Call electronic platform, and the rate is set each day by supply and demand for funds. Banks that are short of cash to meet the cash reserve ratio or large outflows borrow, while those with surplus funds lend. Under the framework as of 2025, the call rate usually stays inside the RBI's corridor, between the standing deposit facility rate at the floor and the marginal standing facility rate at the ceiling, and sits close to the repo rate when liquidity is balanced. That makes it the most direct daily signal of banking-system liquidity. A common confusion: the call money rate is a market rate, not a rate the RBI fixes.
example: Say Bank A has ₹100 crore spare at the end of the day and lends it overnight to Bank B at a call rate of 6.50% a year. Using a 365-day year, Bank B repays ₹100 crore plus ₹100 crore × 6.50% × 1/365, or about ₹1.78 lakh of interest, the next working day.
formula: Overnight interest = Principal × Call rate × 1 / 365

short: The average rate on overnight loans between Indian banks each day, weighted by loan size; the market rate the RBI aims to steer.
kid: Lots of children lend each other coins until tomorrow, some asking for a bit more thanks than others. Mix all those thank-yous together, letting the bigger piles of coins count more, and you get one number for the day.
detail: The weighted average call rate is the volume-weighted average of the interest rates on all overnight call money deals between banks and primary dealers in a day, computed from NDS-Call trades and published by the RBI. Under the framework as of 2025, it is the operating target of Indian monetary policy: the Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate, and the RBI then uses variable rate repo and reverse repo auctions and other liquidity tools to keep the WACR close to it. When banking-system liquidity is in surplus, the WACR tends to drift down towards the standing deposit facility rate; when liquidity is tight, it can rise above the repo rate towards the marginal standing facility rate. A common confusion is to treat the WACR and the repo rate as the same thing: the repo rate is the policy signal, while the WACR shows where overnight money actually trades.
example: Say only two call deals happen in a day: ₹3,000 crore at 6.40% and ₹1,000 crore at 6.60%. The WACR is (3,000 × 6.40 + 1,000 × 6.60) / 4,000 = 25,800 / 4,000 = 6.45%, closer to 6.40% because more money traded at that rate.
formula: WACR = Sum of (Deal amount × Call rate) / Sum of deal amounts

short: The market where banks lend money to, and borrow from, one another, usually for short periods from overnight to a few months.
kid: Shops on the same street help each other: if one runs low on coins for change, a neighbour lends some and gets them back soon, with a tiny thank-you on top.
detail: The interbank market is where banks and some other financial institutions borrow and lend among themselves to manage daily cash, meet reserve requirements and fund short-term needs. Loans may be unsecured, as in India's call money market, or secured against government bonds, as in repo. Rates set here, such as overnight MIBOR in India and the former LIBOR globally, have served as benchmarks for loans and derivatives. The market's health is a key stress signal: when banks doubt one another's solvency, they hoard cash and interbank rates jump relative to policy rates, as in 2008 when lending nearly froze after Lehman Brothers collapsed. Since then, regulators have pushed lending towards secured, centrally cleared markets. The phrase is also used for the interbank foreign exchange market where banks trade currencies, which is why news reports quote the rupee's interbank rate.
example: Say banks can borrow for three months against government bonds at 5.0% but must pay 5.2% to borrow unsecured from other banks. The 0.2 percentage point gap reflects worry about lending to other banks. In October 2008 a similar US measure, the gap between 3-month dollar LIBOR and the overnight index swap rate, rose above 3.5 percentage points.

short: India's benchmark overnight interest rate for lending between banks without security, published every business day by Financial Benchmarks India Ltd (FBIL).
kid: Every morning, someone writes on a board how many extra coins the grown-ups asked for when lending to each other for just one night. Everyone else then uses the number on the board when they make their own promises.
detail: The Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate was launched by the National Stock Exchange in 1998 and has been administered by Financial Benchmarks India Ltd (FBIL) since 2015. Overnight MIBOR is now computed from actual call money trades on the NDS-Call platform in the first hour of trading, rather than from banks' quotes, which makes it harder to manipulate than the old LIBOR. Its biggest use is as the floating leg of overnight indexed swaps (OIS): banks, foreign investors and companies use MIBOR OIS to hedge or take views on Indian interest rates, and OIS rates are read as the market's guess of future RBI moves. Some floating-rate bonds and loans also reference it. A common confusion is to think the RBI sets MIBOR; it is a market rate, though it usually trades close to the repo rate. Regulators have also explored a secured, repo-based overnight benchmark as a future alternative.
example: Say ABC Ltd enters a one-year MIBOR OIS on ₹100 crore, paying a fixed 6.00% and receiving overnight MIBOR compounded over the year. If compounded MIBOR works out to 6.30%, ABC receives the net difference: (6.30% - 6.00%) × ₹100 crore = ₹30 lakh. Had MIBOR compounded to 5.80%, ABC would have paid ₹20 lakh instead.

short: A former benchmark interest rate based on what big banks said they would pay to borrow from each other in London; retired 2021-2024.
kid: Every morning some big children told a teacher how many extra sweets they would want for lending to each other. Some of them fibbed to win games, so the teacher stopped asking and now watches what really happens instead.
detail: LIBOR, the London Interbank Offered Rate, was for decades the world's most important interest rate benchmark, underpinning hundreds of trillions of dollars of loans, bonds and derivatives. Each day a panel of banks submitted the rate at which they believed they could borrow unsecured from other banks, for periods from overnight to one year. Because submissions were estimates rather than real trades, banks could and did manipulate them: the 2012 rigging scandal led to billions of dollars in fines, starting with about $450 million for Barclays. Regulators then moved markets to transaction-based risk-free rates such as SOFR, SONIA and €STR. Most LIBOR settings ended after December 2021, the main US dollar ones after June 2023, and the last temporary synthetic versions in September 2024. In India, MIFOR, which was built on dollar LIBOR, was replaced by a modified version linked to SOFR.
example: Say a company borrowed $10 million at 3-month dollar LIBOR plus 2%. If LIBOR was fixed at 1.5% at the start of a quarter, the loan rate for that quarter was 3.5% a year, so the interest due was about $10 million × 3.5% × 1/4 = $87,500. A similar loan today would typically reference Term SOFR plus a spread instead.

short: The main US dollar benchmark interest rate, measuring the cost of borrowing cash overnight against US government bonds as security.
kid: If you borrow a friend's coins for one night and leave your favourite toy with them until you pay back, they know they are safe. The small extra you pay for that night is what this number measures.
detail: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate has been published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York since April 2018. It is a volume-weighted median of rates on overnight repurchase agreements backed by US Treasury securities, drawn from well over $1 trillion of daily trades in recent years. Chosen by the Alternative Reference Rates Committee in 2017, it replaced US dollar LIBOR in loans, floating-rate notes and swaps. Being secured and based on real trades, SOFR is nearly risk-free and hard to manipulate. Being an overnight rate, it is either compounded over each interest period or replaced by Term SOFR, a forward-looking 1, 3, 6 or 12-month rate derived from futures and published by CME Group. Do not compare it directly with old LIBOR: SOFR has no bank credit risk, so legacy contracts that switched added a fixed spread, about 0.26 percentage point for 3-month LIBOR.
example: Say a company has a $20 million loan at 3-month Term SOFR plus 2.00%, and Term SOFR is set at 4.00% for the coming quarter. The loan rate is 6.00%, and on the US convention of a 360-day year, interest for 90 days is $20 million × 6.00% × 90/360 = $300,000.
formula: Loan rate = SOFR (compounded, or Term SOFR) + Fixed credit spread

short: The UK's benchmark interest rate for overnight sterling borrowing between banks and other big financial firms, published daily by the Bank of England.
kid: In Britain, big money houses lend each other money for just one night. Every day someone looks at what they all asked in return and writes down the usual amount, so everyone can use the same number.
detail: SONIA, the Sterling Overnight Index Average, measures the average rate at which banks pay to borrow sterling overnight, unsecured, from other financial institutions such as money market funds. The Bank of England has administered it since 2016 and, after a 2018 reform, calculates it as a volume-weighted trimmed mean of eligible deals, using the middle 50% by volume. It was chosen in 2017 as the UK's preferred risk-free rate and replaced sterling LIBOR, which ended after 2021, in loans, floating-rate notes and swaps. SONIA tracks the Bank of England's Bank Rate closely, so it moves mainly with monetary policy rather than with worries about bank credit. A common confusion is to group it with SOFR as a secured rate: SONIA is unsecured, while SOFR is based on repo trades backed by bonds. Like other overnight rates, it is compounded over each interest period when used in term loans.
example: Say a bank places £10 million overnight with another firm at a SONIA-level rate of 4.00%. Sterling uses a 365-day year, so the interest earned is £10 million × 4.00% × 1/365, or about £1,096 for the night.

short: The euro area's benchmark overnight interest rate, measuring what banks pay to borrow euros overnight without security, published daily by the European Central Bank.
kid: In many countries that share one kind of coin, big money houses borrow from each other for one night. Every morning a helper writes down the usual price of that one-night borrowing for everyone to see.
detail: The euro short-term rate, written €STR, has been published by the European Central Bank each business day since October 2019. It reflects the wholesale cost of overnight unsecured borrowing in euros by euro area banks, calculated as a volume-weighted trimmed mean of deals reported to the ECB under its money market statistical reporting. It replaced EONIA, which was redefined as €STR plus 8.5 basis points in 2019 and discontinued in January 2022, and it is the risk-free reference rate for euro swaps. €STR normally sits a little below the ECB's deposit facility rate, because much of the borrowing is from money market funds and other non-banks that cannot deposit at the central bank. A common confusion is to treat €STR as having replaced EURIBOR: EURIBOR still exists as a term rate, and €STR serves as its fallback and as the main swap benchmark.
example: Say a bank borrows €100 million overnight at a €STR-level rate of 2.00%. Euro money markets use a 360-day year, so the interest is €100 million × 2.00% × 1/360, or about €5,556 for the night.

short: A benchmark rate for euro loans between banks, without security, for one week to twelve months; used to price many European mortgages and loans.
kid: Many families borrowed coins to buy their house, and they give a little extra back each month. How big that little extra is goes up and down with one special number written down every day.
detail: EURIBOR, the Euro Interbank Offered Rate, is administered by the European Money Markets Institute in Brussels and published each business day for 1-week, 1-month, 3-month, 6-month and 12-month terms. Since 2019 it has used a hybrid method that relies on actual transactions where available and falls back to related market data and modelled estimates, which brought it in line with EU benchmark rules. Unlike LIBOR, EURIBOR was reformed rather than scrapped, so it still sets the rate on millions of variable-rate mortgages in countries such as Spain and Portugal, as well as on corporate loans and swaps. It moves with expectations for ECB policy plus a small premium for bank credit and term risk, so it usually sits above €STR for the same horizon. A common confusion is to think all interbank offered rates ended with LIBOR; EURIBOR continues, with €STR as its fallback.
example: Say a household has a €200,000 mortgage at 12-month EURIBOR plus 1%. If EURIBOR resets from 3.5% to 2.5%, the loan rate falls from 4.5% to 3.5%, and the next year's interest on €200,000, ignoring repayments, drops from €9,000 to €7,000.
formula: Loan rate = EURIBOR for the chosen term + Fixed margin

short: The interest rate on money borrowed today and repaid on the next business day; it is the rate central banks steer most directly.
kid: If you borrow a friend's crayons after school and give them back the next morning, that is a one-night borrow. The tiny thank-you you give for that one night is like this rate.
detail: The overnight rate is the interest rate on loans that mature on the next business day, whether unsecured between banks or secured against bonds in repo. It is where monetary policy acts first: most central banks steer an overnight rate, such as the federal funds rate in the US, €STR in the euro area, the overnight rate in Canada and the weighted average call rate in India. Changes then pass through to longer money market rates, bond yields and bank lending rates. Overnight rates also reveal day-to-day liquidity: a spike signals a cash shortage, as in the US repo turmoil of September 2019. They are quoted as annualised percentages, so the interest for a single night is tiny. A common trap is the weekend: a loan taken on Friday and repaid on Monday earns three days of interest.
example: Say a bank borrows ₹200 crore on a Friday at an overnight rate of 6% a year and repays it on Monday. Interest runs for three days: ₹200 crore × 6% × 3/365, or about ₹9.86 lakh.
formula: Interest = Principal × Overnight rate × Number of days / 365 (360 in some markets)

short: A short-term loan in which one party sells bonds and agrees to buy them back later at a slightly higher price.
kid: You give your friend your toy car and get some coins today. Tomorrow you give the coins back plus one extra, and you get your car back.
detail: In a repurchase agreement, or repo, a borrower sells securities, usually government bonds, to a lender for cash and promises to buy them back on a set date at a higher price. The price difference is the interest, and its annualised value is the repo rate for that deal. Economically it is a collateralised loan: the securities protect the lender if the borrower defaults, and lenders often apply a haircut, lending a little less than the collateral is worth. The same deal seen from the lender's side is a reverse repo. Repos fund bond dealers and banks and let money market funds park cash safely. In India, market repo and TREPS deals are mostly in G-secs and T-bills, alongside a smaller corporate bond repo market. Do not confuse market repo deals with the RBI's policy repo rate, the rate at which the RBI lends to banks in its liquidity operations.
example: Say a mutual fund lends ₹99 crore to a bond dealer for 7 days against G-secs worth ₹100 crore, a 1% haircut, at a repo rate of 6.5% a year. The dealer buys the bonds back for ₹99 crore × (1 + 6.5% × 7/365), or about ₹99.12 crore, so the fund earns roughly ₹12.34 lakh.
formula: Repurchase price = Sale price × (1 + Repo rate × Days / Day-count basis), where the basis is 365 in India and 360 in the US

short: A major Indian money market for short-term lending against government bonds, run by the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL), which guarantees every trade.
kid: Two children want to swap coins for a toy and swap back tomorrow, but they do not know each other well. A trusted teacher holds the toy, keeps track and makes sure everyone gets back what they should.
detail: TREPS, short for Tri-party Repo Dealing and Settlement, is a repo market in government securities operated by the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL). It replaced the older collateralised borrowing and lending obligation (CBLO) from November 2018. In a tri-party repo, a third party, here CCIL, handles collateral selection, valuation, margins and settlement, and also acts as central counterparty, so lenders face CCIL rather than the individual borrower. Trades are anonymous and mostly overnight. Mutual funds, especially liquid and overnight funds, are major lenders, while banks and primary dealers are big borrowers. In recent years TREPS volumes have been far larger than call money volumes, making the TREPS rate a key gauge of liquidity; it often trades a little below the call rate because it is secured. When reading a debt fund's portfolio, a line marked TREPS is simply cash lent overnight, not a risky holding.
example: Say a liquid fund has ₹1,000 crore of spare cash at the end of the day and lends it overnight on TREPS at 6.20% a year. The next day it gets back ₹1,000 crore plus ₹1,000 crore × 6.20% × 1/365, or about ₹16.99 lakh of interest, with CCIL guaranteeing the deal.

short: A short-term IOU, usually for up to one year, that large, highly rated companies sell to investors to borrow money without pledging any assets.
kid: A big lemonade stand needs coins today to buy lemons. It writes a promise note saying it will pay back a bit more in a few weeks, and people who trust it hand over their coins.
detail: Commercial paper is an unsecured, short-term promissory note issued by companies, NBFCs and financial institutions to fund working capital and other short-term needs. It is usually issued at a discount to face value and repaid at face value, so the difference is the investor's return. Under the rules as of 2025, Indian CPs must carry a credit rating and run from 7 days to one year; in the US most CP matures within 270 days to avoid registration with the SEC. Buyers are mainly mutual funds, banks and corporate treasuries. Because nothing backs it except the issuer's credit, CP is only as safe as the issuer and depends on a steady market for rollover: when IL&FS defaulted on its CP and other debt in September 2018, CP funding for many NBFCs dried up. Do not confuse CP with a certificate of deposit, which is issued by banks.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues 91-day CP with a face value of ₹5 lakh per unit at a price of ₹4,92,000. An investor earns ₹8,000 per unit, an annualised yield of (8,000 / 4,92,000) × 365/91, or about 6.52%.
formula: Yield = (Face value - Issue price) / Issue price × 365 / Days to maturity

short: A fixed-term, fixed-rate bank deposit; in India, a tradable short-term instrument banks sell to large investors to raise funds.
kid: You give your piggy bank coins to a grown-up who promises to keep them safe for a set time. When the time is up, you get your coins back with a few extra.
detail: A certificate of deposit is a time deposit with a fixed maturity and interest rate, documented so that it can be transferred. In India, CDs are negotiable money market instruments issued by scheduled commercial banks for 7 days to one year, and by select all-India financial institutions for one to three years, under the rules as of 2025. They are issued at a discount, in dematerialised form, mainly to mutual funds, companies and other institutions, and can be traded before maturity. Banks lean on CDs when deposit growth lags loan growth, so heavy CD issuance and rising CD rates signal tight bank funding. In the US, by contrast, a CD is mostly a retail time deposit, often insured by the FDIC, with a penalty for early withdrawal. A common confusion in India is to equate CDs with fixed deposits: FDs are non-tradable retail deposits, while CDs are wholesale and tradable.
example: Say a bank issues a 182-day CD with a face value of ₹5 lakh at a price of ₹4,85,000. The buyer receives ₹5 lakh at maturity, earning ₹15,000, an annualised yield of (15,000 / 4,85,000) × 365/182, or about 6.20%.
formula: Yield = (Face value - Issue price) / Issue price × 365 / Days to maturity

short: A contract that fixes today the interest rate for a loan period starting in the future, settled by paying only the difference in cash.
kid: You and a friend agree today on how many sweets borrowing a toy will cost next month. If the usual price changes by then, one of you just gives the other the difference.
detail: A forward rate agreement is an over-the-counter contract in which two parties agree to exchange the difference between a fixed rate and a floating reference rate on a notional amount for a future period. A 3x6 FRA, for example, covers a three-month period that begins three months from now. No principal changes hands: when the period starts, the interest difference is paid in cash, discounted because it is paid upfront rather than at the period's end. The buyer, who pays the fixed rate, gains if rates rise, so a company planning to borrow later can buy an FRA to lock in its cost, while an investor planning to deposit funds can sell one. FRAs are building blocks for pricing swaps and reading the market's rate expectations. A common confusion is to think an FRA is a loan: it only fixes the rate, and the actual borrowing happens separately.
example: Say a company buys a 3x6 FRA on a $10 million notional at 4.00%. In three months the reference rate for the 90-day period is set at 4.50%, so the company is owed $10 million × (4.50% - 4.00%) × 90/360 = $12,500, which is discounted for early payment to $12,500 / (1 + 4.50% × 90/360), or about $12,361.
formula: FRA payment = Notional × (Reference rate - FRA rate) × (Days / 360) / (1 + Reference rate × Days / 360)

short: The fixed interest rate the market will exchange for a floating rate over a chosen period; the price of an interest rate swap.
kid: Two friends agree to trade: one gives the same number of sweets every week, the other gives a number that changes with the weather. The steady number that makes the trade fair for both is what this word means.
detail: In a plain interest rate swap, one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays a floating rate, such as SOFR in the US or overnight MIBOR in India, on the same notional amount. The swap rate is the fixed rate that makes the present value of the fixed payments equal the expected present value of the floating payments, so the swap is worth zero at the start. Plotting swap rates across maturities gives the swap curve, which banks use to price fixed-rate loans and to hedge. Because the floating leg follows expected policy rates, swap rates show where markets think rates are heading; in India, OIS rates are the clearest market signal of expected RBI moves. The gap between a swap rate and the same-maturity government bond yield is the swap spread. A common confusion is to call the swap rate a borrowing rate: no principal is lent.
example: Say a company has a $50 million five-year floating loan at SOFR plus 1.5% and fears rising rates. It enters a five-year swap, paying the 3.8% swap rate and receiving SOFR, so its cost is fixed at 3.8% + 1.5% = 5.3%, or $50 million × 5.3% = $2.65 million a year, whatever SOFR does.
formula: Par swap rate = (1 - DFn) / Sum of (Accrual fraction i × DFi), where DFi is the discount factor for payment date i and n is the final date

short: Exchange-traded contracts that settle on the average US federal funds rate for a future month, showing what markets expect the Federal Reserve to do.
kid: Children guess how many sweets the teacher will hand out next month and agree on that guess today. Looking at everyone's guesses tells you what they think the teacher will do.
detail: Fed funds futures, traded on CME Group's Chicago Board of Trade, are cash-settled contracts on the average daily effective federal funds rate over a calendar month. The price is quoted as 100 minus the expected average rate, so a price of 95.75 implies an expected average of 4.25%. Banks and investors use them to hedge short-term rate risk, but their best-known use is as a window into market expectations: by comparing contracts for months before and after each FOMC meeting, analysts back out the probability of a rate cut or hike, as the CME FedWatch tool does. When news says markets are pricing in a cut, these futures are usually the source. A common confusion is to treat the implied path as a Fed forecast or a certainty: it is a market price that includes risk premiums and can swing sharply after a single data release.
example: Say the September fed funds futures contract trades at 95.80. The implied average effective fed funds rate for September is 100 - 95.80 = 4.20%. If the rate stood at 4.33% going into the month, the lower implied average suggests traders expect a cut by or during September.
formula: Implied average rate (%) = 100 - Futures price

short: The base interest rate US banks charge their most creditworthy borrowers, used as the starting point for many consumer and small-business loans.
kid: A shop gives its best, most trusted customers the lowest price. Everyone else pays that price plus a little extra, depending on how much the shop trusts them.
detail: The prime rate is the benchmark lending rate US commercial banks set for their best customers. By long-standing convention it equals the upper end of the Federal Reserve's federal funds target range plus 3 percentage points, and the widely quoted Wall Street Journal Prime Rate changes when most large US banks change theirs, usually right after an FOMC decision. Credit cards, home equity lines of credit and many small-business loans are priced at prime plus a margin, so a Fed move passes straight through to these borrowers. Despite the name, the biggest companies often borrow below prime through bonds or SOFR-based loans. India's old prime lending rate gave way to the base rate in 2010 and MCLR in 2016, and since October 2019 new floating-rate retail loans have been linked to external benchmarks such as the repo rate. Do not confuse the prime rate with the Fed's own policy rate.
example: Say the Fed's target range is 4.25% to 4.50%. The prime rate would then be 4.50% + 3% = 7.50%, and a credit card priced at prime plus 14 percentage points would charge 7.50% + 14% = 21.50% a year. A 0.25 point Fed cut would lower both by 0.25 point.
formula: US prime rate = Upper bound of the fed funds target range + 3 percentage points (market convention)
related: Marginal cost of funds based lending rate

short: A published interest rate that floating-rate loans, bonds and other contracts are linked to, so their payments move up and down with it.
kid: Imagine a sign at the school gate that shows a number each day. Many families agree that what they pay each other will go up or down whenever the number on the sign changes.
detail: A reference rate, or interest rate benchmark, is an independently published rate used to reset the interest on floating-rate instruments: a loan might pay the reference rate plus a fixed spread. Good benchmarks are transparent, hard to manipulate and based on real transactions. Examples include SOFR, SONIA and €STR, which are overnight risk-free rates; EURIBOR, a term bank rate; and in India overnight MIBOR, T-bill rates and the RBI repo rate, which since October 2019 has been the most common external benchmark for floating-rate home loans. Benchmark reform means the global shift, after the LIBOR scandal and the 2013 IOSCO principles, from bank-estimated rates to transaction-based ones. In India, FBIL administers several benchmarks under RBI oversight. In news, the term also covers FBIL's daily rupee-dollar reference rate, which is an exchange rate benchmark rather than an interest rate.
example: Say a ₹50 lakh home loan is priced at the RBI repo rate plus 2.75 percentage points. If the repo rate is 6.00%, the loan rate is 8.75% and first-year interest is roughly ₹50 lakh × 8.75% = ₹4,37,500, ignoring repayments. If the RBI cuts the repo rate by 0.25 point, the loan rate resets to 8.50% at the next reset date.
formula: Floating rate = Reference rate + Fixed spread

short: The true yearly interest rate after counting interest earned on interest during the year; it lets you compare loans and deposits fairly.
kid: If your piggy bank gets one extra coin every month, those new coins start earning extra coins too. So by the end of the year you have a bit more than you first thought.
detail: The effective annual rate is the interest rate actually earned or paid over a year once compounding is taken into account. A nominal rate of 12% a year compounded monthly really means 1% a month, and because each month's interest itself earns interest, the effective rate is about 12.68%. The more often interest compounds, the higher the effective rate for the same nominal rate, with continuous compounding as the upper limit. EAR is the right way to compare products that compound at different frequencies, such as a fixed deposit compounding quarterly against a bond paying every six months, or to see the true cost of a credit card that quotes a monthly rate. A common confusion is with the annual percentage rate (APR), which often just multiplies the periodic rate by the number of periods and so understates the true cost.
example: Say a credit card charges 3.5% a month. Multiplying by 12 gives a nominal 42% a year, but the effective annual rate is (1 + 0.035)^12 - 1, or about 51.1%. Similarly, a deposit paying 12% a year compounded monthly has an EAR of (1.01)^12 - 1, or about 12.68%.
formula: EAR = (1 + Nominal rate / m)^m - 1, where m is the number of compounding periods per year; with continuous compounding, EAR = e^r - 1

short: Labels for how the gap between short-term and long-term bond yields changes, and whether yields are falling (bull) or rising (bear) as it does.
kid: Picture a slide with a low end and a high end. The slide can get steeper or flatter, and that can happen because one end rises or because one end sinks. Each way has its own nickname.
detail: These four terms describe yield curve moves by combining shape and direction. Steepening means the gap between long-term and short-term yields widens; flattening means it narrows. Bull means bond prices are rising, so yields are falling; bear means prices are falling and yields rising. A bull steepening, with short yields falling faster, usually comes when markets expect rate cuts. A bear steepening, with long yields rising faster, points to worries about inflation, heavy government borrowing or a higher term premium. A bull flattening, with long yields falling faster, often reflects growth fears or a rush to safety, while a bear flattening, with short yields rising faster, is typical when a central bank is hiking. Traders usually compare 2-year and 10-year yields, or 10-year and 30-year. A common confusion is assuming bull and bear refer to stocks here: they refer to bond prices.
example: Say the 2-year yield falls from 4.0% to 3.6% while the 10-year falls only from 4.2% to 4.1%. Both yields fell, which is bullish for bonds, and the 10-year minus 2-year gap widened from 0.2 to 0.5 percentage point. That is a bull steepening of 30 basis points.
formula: Curve slope = Long-term yield - Short-term yield (for example, 10-year minus 2-year)

short: The gap between the fixed rate on an interest rate swap and the government bond yield of the same maturity.
kid: Two friends each promise to give you sweets every week for a year. One is the head teacher and one is a classmate. The small difference between what they promise is this gap.
detail: The swap spread is the swap rate minus the yield on a government bond of the same maturity, for example the 10-year SOFR swap rate minus the 10-year US Treasury yield. It used to be clearly positive because swaps were tied to LIBOR, which carried bank credit risk, while governments were seen as safer borrowers. Today it mainly reflects supply and demand: heavy government bond issuance, dealers' limited balance sheets under post-2008 capital rules, and pension funds receiving fixed in swaps can push it below zero. The US 30-year swap spread has been negative almost continuously since late 2008, and the 10-year for most of the time since 2015. Traders bet on it directly, and sharp moves can signal stress in Treasury funding. A common confusion is to read a negative spread as the market judging banks safer than the government: it reflects balance sheet and supply effects, not credit.
example: Say the 10-year SOFR swap rate is 3.90% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.30%. The swap spread is 3.90% - 4.30% = -0.40 percentage point, or -40 basis points. If heavy Treasury issuance lifts the Treasury yield to 4.40% while the swap rate stays put, the spread becomes more negative, at -50 basis points.
formula: Swap spread = Swap rate - Government bond yield of the same maturity

short: A free CME Group tool that converts prices of US interest rate futures into the odds markets give each possible Federal Reserve rate decision.
kid: Before the class votes on a picnic, children put marbles in jars to show what they think will happen. Counting the marbles shows how likely everyone thinks a yes or a no is.
detail: CME FedWatch, published by CME Group, estimates the probability of each possible outcome at upcoming Federal Open Market Committee meetings, such as a hold or a 25 basis point cut, from the prices of 30-Day Fed Funds futures. It works out the average rate implied for the month of a meeting, separates the days before and after the decision, and converts the implied change into odds between neighbouring outcomes. News stories saying traders see a 70% chance of a cut are usually quoting FedWatch. Because Fed expectations move the dollar, US yields and global capital flows, Indian markets watch it too. Treat it with care: the odds come from prices that include risk premiums, assume standard-sized moves, and can swing sharply on a single data release. It is a summary of market pricing, not a forecast by the Fed or by CME.
example: Say the effective fed funds rate is 4.33% and a 25 basis point cut would take it to 4.08%. If futures imply an average rate of 4.18% after the meeting, the implied probability of a cut is (4.33 - 4.18) / (4.33 - 4.08) = 0.15 / 0.25 = 60%, leaving a 40% chance of no change.
formula: Probability of a move = (Current rate - Implied post-meeting rate) / (Current rate - Rate after the move)
